## The idea

An ear drill should make a clear demand and produce evidence about the answer. If the prompt is too broad, the pause too short, or the trial distribution hidden, a final score says little about what you can recognize. Owning the code makes each of those conditions inspectable.

The program below chooses a seeded random root and an interval distance from a configurable pool. It plays the ascending pair, leaves four beats for an answer, then prints the standard name and replays the sound. The prompt comes before the label so recognition has to occur without visual help. The replay joins feedback to the exact sound that prompted the decision.

The pool also controls emphasis. Repeating a distance makes it more likely to appear, allowing a difficult interval to receive extra trials without changing the playback loop.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_random_seed 42
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

names = {2 => "major second", 4 => "major third", 7 => "perfect fifth", 12 => "octave"}
pool = [2, 4, 7, 12, 7]

10.times do |trial|
  root = rrand_i(note(:c3), note(:b4))
  distance = pool.choose
  play root, release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play root + distance, release: 0.7
  sleep 4
  puts "trial #{trial + 1}: #{names[distance]}"
  play root; sleep 0.75; play root + distance
  sleep 2
end
```

Each trial presents an ascending interval at a root somewhere between C3 and B4. Four beats provide response time; at 72 BPM, that is a little over three seconds. The log then reveals the name and the pair sounds again. The fixed seed reproduces the session only while the random calls and their source collections stay unchanged. A pause edit preserves the sequence; a weighting edit changes the pool and can remap later draws.

## Change one thing

1. Repeat the distance you miss most in `pool`. Before running the drill, calculate its new share of the array. The extra copy raises probability without changing how a trial is rendered.

2. Restore the pool and shorten the answer pause from four beats to two. Record whether you can still name the sound before the reveal or begin responding to time pressure instead of the interval.

3. Restore the four-beat pause and restrict roots to one octave. After ten trials, widen the range again. Compare errors by distance to see whether recognition depends on a familiar register.

## Why it works

The drill resembles a small test runner. The `names` hash defines the valid cases and their expected labels. The pool defines both scope and sampling weight. Root selection varies the fixture, the answer pause creates an unassisted response window, and the reveal supplies feedback.

A fixed random seed is development equipment. It makes chosen roots and distances repeat when the call order and collections are unchanged, so a timing edit can be assessed against known trials. Weighting or range edits alter those mappings and should be treated as newly reproducible sessions rather than identical prompts. For actual practice, different seeds broaden the material. Record the seed whenever you intend to reproduce a surprising error.

Weighting by duplication is transparent in a five-item pool: the fifth has two entries and is therefore chosen twice as often as each other distance. As the trainer grows, explicit counts or probabilities may communicate policy more clearly. Whatever representation you choose, print or log it. A score without its sampling distribution cannot explain the session's difficulty.

Session totals are also insufficient on their own. A result of nine out of ten may contain no octave trial, or it may contain five fifths because the pool is weighted. Count prompts, correct answers, and misses by distance. When the pool changes, retain the old distribution beside the score so an apparent improvement cannot be explained by an easier sample.

The reveal phase needs enough separation from the prompt to prevent accidental cueing, yet a very long pause makes each trial cumbersome. Treat the four-beat value as a parameter to audition. The right duration allows a complete decision and a recorded answer before feedback begins.

The distance arrays in this interval drill also prepare the next construction.
Lesson 21 will arrange interval steps into a scale formula, turning the same
semitone arithmetic from isolated prompts into an ordered route through a key.
Later drills for scales, chords, and cadences reuse the generator, response
window, replay, and logged evidence even as their label sets change.

## Take it further

Run a ten-trial session from four ascending intervals and write each answer before its reveal. Extend the program or use a nearby text record to capture the date, pool, seed, ten prompts, ten answers, correctness by distance, and total score. Keep accidental input errors distinguishable from genuine recognition misses.

Add a fifth interval only after scores of at least nine out of ten in two consecutive sessions under the same distribution. Record whether that expansion rule fired. Before treating the drill as training data, audition its answer pause, replay level, and root range in Sonic Pi 5. The resulting record should explain both what was tested and why the pool changed next.
